Pattern 05 of 15

LinkedList In-place Reversal

Reverse a linked list (or just a piece of it) by flipping each arrow to point backwards, one node at a time, using three pointers and no extra memory.

1. What is this pattern for?

Picture a conga line where each dancer holds the shoulder of the person in front. To make the line face the other way, you walk down it and tell each dancer, one by one, to let go and grab the person who was behind them instead. You only ever need to remember three people: the one you just turned around (prev_node), the one you're turning now (current), and the next one in line (next_node), so you don't lose the rest of the line when current lets go.

A singly linked list is a chain of nodes where each node knows only its next. You can't index into it or walk backwards. The in-place reversal pattern rewires the next pointers so the chain points the other way, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space (no copying into an array).

It's the building block for: reversing the whole list, reversing positions left..right, reversing every group of k, swapping pairs, and "compare the first half with the reversed second half" problems (palindrome, twin sums, reorder).

2. How it works (bisected)

  1. Set up. prev_node = None (the new tail will point at nothing), current = head.
  2. Save. next_node = current.next. Do this first, because the next line destroys your only link to the rest of the list.
  3. Flip. current.next = prev_node. The arrow now points backwards.
  4. Advance both. prev_node = current, then current = next_node. Repeat steps 2–4 until current is None.
  5. Return prev_node: it's the old tail, now the new head.
  6. Level up: reverse just a part. Use a dummy node before the head so "the node before the part" always exists (even when the part starts at the head). Remember the node just before the part and the part's first node (it'll become the part's tail), reverse the part, then stitch both ends back.

Naming note: the code on this page uses the long names prev_node, current and next_node. The animations below have little room for labels, so they shorten them to prev, cur and nxt. They are the same three pointers.

3. Seeing a problem: how to spot In-place Reversal

Trigger words

  • "reverse the linked list", "reverse from position left to right"
  • "reverse nodes in k-group", "swap every two adjacent nodes"
  • "in place", "O(1) extra memory", "do not modify the values, only the nodes"
  • "palindrome linked list", "twin sum", "reorder list", "add two numbers II" (when the digits are stored in an inconvenient order)

Shape of the input

  • A singly linked list (ListNode with val and next).
  • You need to traverse it in the opposite order, or reorder blocks of nodes.
  • Brute-force smell: "copy all values into a Python list, reverse/re-arrange, write them back". That's O(n) extra space, and often forbidden ("don't change values").
The one question to ask"Would this be easy if (part of) the list pointed the other way?" If yes, flip it in place with prev_node / current / next_node.

4. When to use it, and when not to

Use In-place Reversal when…Prefer something else when…
You must reverse all or part of a linked list in O(1) spaceSpace doesn't matter and clarity does: push nodes onto a stack or into an array
Comparing the first half with the second half backwards (palindrome, twin sum)You only need the middle or a cycle: that's Fast & Slow Pointers (often used together: find middle, then reverse)
Reordering blocks of nodes (k-group, swap pairs)You have an array: reversing a slice is just Two Pointers swapping from both ends
Reversal must not allocate new nodesYou're merging sorted lists: use a dummy + splice (or a heap for k lists, see Top-K)

Cost: O(n) time (each node's arrow is flipped once), O(1) extra space. The recursive version is also O(n) time but uses O(n) call-stack space.

5. The Python template (memorize this)

# A) Reverse the whole list with three pointers.
def reverse(head):
    # prev_node = the front of the part we have ALREADY reversed.
    # Nothing is reversed yet, so it starts as None
    # (the old head becomes the new tail, and a tail points at None).
    prev_node = None
    # current = the node whose arrow we are about to flip.
    current = head
    # Keep going until we walk off the end of the list.
    while current is not None:
        # 1. SAVE the rest of the list. The next line overwrites
        #    current.next, and without this we would lose the rest forever.
        next_node = current.next
        # 2. FLIP the arrow: current now points backwards.
        current.next = prev_node
        # 3. STEP prev_node forward: current is the new front of the reversed part.
        prev_node = current
        # 4. STEP current forward: move on to the saved rest of the list.
        current = next_node
    # current is None now. prev_node is the old tail, which is the new head.
    return prev_node


# B) Reverse only positions left..right (1-indexed) with a dummy node
#    and "head insertion".
def reverse_between(head, left, right):
    # A dummy node in front of head guarantees that a node BEFORE the part
    # always exists, even when left == 1.
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    # Walk left - 1 steps so that 'before' stops just before position left.
    before = dummy
    for step in range(left - 1):
        before = before.next
    # tail = the first node of the part. It never moves itself;
    # the other nodes jump over it, so it ends up LAST in the part.
    tail = before.next
    # right - left moves are enough to reverse the part.
    for move in range(right - left):
        # The node right after tail is the one we move this time.
        moved = tail.next
        # Unhook it: tail now skips over it.
        tail.next = moved.next
        # Insert it at the FRONT of the part, right after 'before'.
        moved.next = before.next
        before.next = moved
    # dummy.next is the real head (it changed if left was 1).
    return dummy.next

The same template, explained for a beginner:

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Template A, set up: prev_node = None because nothing has been reversed yet (and the old head, which becomes the new tail, must point at None). current = head is the first node whose arrow we will flip.
  2. while current is not None: repeat until we have walked off the end of the list.
  3. Save: next_node = current.next remembers the rest of the list. This must come first, because the next line overwrites current.next.
  4. Flip: current.next = prev_node turns the arrow around, so current now points back at the already-reversed part.
  5. Step, step: prev_node = current (the reversed part grew by one node) and current = next_node (move on to the saved rest).
  6. return prev_node: when current is None, prev_node is the old last node, which is the new head.
  7. Template B, set up: dummy = ListNode(0, head) puts a fake node in front, so there is always a node before the part, even when left == 1.
  8. for step in range(left - 1): before = before.next walks to the node just before position left.
  9. tail = before.next is the first node of the part. It never moves itself: the other nodes jump in front of it, so it ends up last.
  10. for move in range(right - left): each move takes moved = tail.next, unhooks it (tail.next = moved.next) and inserts it at the front of the part (moved.next = before.next, then before.next = moved).
  11. return dummy.next: the real head (it is a different node if left was 1).

6. How to remember it forever

Memory hook: "Save, flip, step, step"Four lines, always in this order: next_node = current.next → current.next = prev_node → prev_node = current → current = next_node. Each line's left side is the previous line's right side, like a chain.

Picture

A row of dominoes with arrows. Your hand moves left to right, turning each arrow around. Behind your hand is a reversed list (prev_node is its head); ahead is the untouched rest (next_node).

Chant

"Save the next, point back, prev_node steps up, current steps on."

Dummy rule

"If the head might change, start with a dummy." Then return dummy.next.

7. LeetCode problems, solved step by step

Hard 25. Reverse Nodes in k-Group

Problem: Reverse the nodes of the list k at a time. If the last group has fewer than k nodes, leave it as it is. Only change links, not values.

Spot it: "reverse" + "k at a time" + "only nodes may be changed": repeated sub-list reversal with stitching.

Key insight: keep group_prev (the node before the group). First check that k nodes exist (find kth). Reverse the group with prev_node initialised to group_next instead of None: that way the group's old first node automatically points to the rest of the list. Then hook group_prev.next = kth and move group_prev to the old first node (now the group's tail).

Approach:

  1. Make a dummy before head; group_prev = dummy.
  2. Walk k steps from group_prev to find kth. If you hit None, return dummy.next.
  3. Save group_next = kth.next. Reverse the k nodes with prev_node starting at group_next.
  4. Stitch: group_prev.next = kth (the new front). The old first node is now the group's tail, so it becomes the next group_prev.
  5. Repeat.
class Solution:
    def reverseKGroup(self, head: Optional[ListNode], k: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # The head changes after the first group, so put a dummy in front.
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        # group_prev = the node just BEFORE the group we are working on.
        group_prev = dummy
        while True:
            # --- 1) Is there a full group of k nodes? ---
            # Walk k steps from group_prev. We land on the k-th node of the group.
            kth = group_prev
            for step in range(k):
                kth = kth.next
                if kth is None:
                    # Fewer than k nodes are left: leave them as they are.
                    return dummy.next
            # The first node AFTER this group (it may be None).
            group_next = kth.next
            # The group's first node. After reversing, it will be the group's LAST node.
            group_first = group_prev.next

            # --- 2) Reverse the k nodes of this group (save, flip, step, step). ---
            # Trick: prev_node starts at group_next instead of None, so the old
            # first node automatically ends up pointing at the rest of the list.
            prev_node = group_next
            current = group_first
            while current is not group_next:
                next_node = current.next      # save the rest
                current.next = prev_node      # flip the arrow
                prev_node = current           # step prev_node
                current = next_node           # step current

            # --- 3) Stitch the front of the group back in. ---
            # kth was the group's last node; now it is the group's first node.
            group_prev.next = kth
            # The old first node is now the group's tail, so it is
            # the node BEFORE the next group.
            group_prev = group_first

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. dummy = ListNode(0, head) and group_prev = dummy: the head will change after the first group, so we keep a fake node in front. group_prev always sits just before the group we are working on.
  2. while True: handle one group per round. The only way out is the return inside.
  3. Check for a full group: starting at group_prev, the for step in range(k) loop walks k nodes. If it falls off the end (kth is None), fewer than k nodes are left, so we stop and return dummy.next without touching them.
  4. group_next = kth.next is the first node after the group; group_first = group_prev.next is the group's first node (it will become the group's last node).
  5. Reverse the group: the usual save / flip / step / step loop, with one trick: prev_node starts at group_next instead of None. So when group_first is flipped, it points straight at the rest of the list and the back end is already stitched. The loop stops when current reaches group_next.
  6. group_prev.next = kth stitches the front: the node before the group now points at the old last node, which is the new first node.
  7. group_prev = group_first: the old first node is now the group's tail, so it is the node before the next group.

Dry run on LeetCode example head = [1,2,3,4,5], k = 2 (expected [2,1,4,3,5]):

Roundgroup_prevkthgroup_nextlist after stitching
group 1dummy232 → 1 → 3 → 4 → 5 (new group_prev = 1)
group 21452 → 1 → 4 → 3 → 5 (new group_prev = 3)
check 33None (ran out)—fewer than k nodes left → return 2 → 1 → 4 → 3 → 5

Complexity: O(n) time (each node visited twice), O(1) space.

Medium 92. Reverse Linked List II

Problem: Reverse only positions left..right (1-indexed) of the list, in one pass.

Spot it: "reverse from position left to right". Partial reversal: needs a dummy (left may be 1) and stitching. The second visualizer above traces it.

Key insight: "head insertion": the part's first node (tail) stays put while each following node is unhooked and moved to the front of the part. After right − left moves, the part is reversed and both ends are already connected.

Approach:

  1. Create a dummy before head and walk left − 1 steps to reach before.
  2. tail = before.next: the part's first node, which will end up last.
  3. Repeat right − left times: unhook moved = tail.next and insert it right after before.
  4. Return dummy.next.
class Solution:
    def reverseBetween(self, head: Optional[ListNode], left: int, right: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # A dummy node in front of head: a node before the part always exists,
        # even when left == 1.
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        # Walk left - 1 steps so that 'before' stops just before position left.
        before = dummy
        for step in range(left - 1):
            before = before.next
        # tail = first node of the part. It stays where it is while the other
        # nodes are moved in front of it, so it ends up last.
        tail = before.next
        # Do right - left moves.
        for move in range(right - left):
            # The node right after tail is the one we move.
            moved = tail.next
            # Unhook it: tail skips over it.
            tail.next = moved.next
            # Insert it at the front of the part (right after 'before').
            moved.next = before.next
            before.next = moved
        # dummy.next is the real head (it changed if left was 1).
        return dummy.next

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. dummy = ListNode(0, head): a fake node before the head, so the node before the part always exists (needed when left == 1).
  2. before = dummy, then for step in range(left - 1): before = before.next walks to the node just before position left.
  3. tail = before.next: the first node of the part. It stays put while the nodes after it are moved in front of it, so it ends up last.
  4. for move in range(right - left): a part of right - left + 1 nodes needs right - left moves.
  5. moved = tail.next picks the node right after tail; tail.next = moved.next unhooks it (tail skips over it).
  6. moved.next = before.next and before.next = moved insert it at the front of the part, right after before.
  7. return dummy.next: the real head of the list.

Dry run on LeetCode example head = [1,2,3,4,5], left = 2, right = 4 (expected [1,4,3,2,5]):

Stepbeforetailmovedlist (from dummy.next)
setup12—1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5
move 11231 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5
move 21241 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 5
returndummy.next → 1 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 5

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 24. Swap Nodes in Pairs

Problem: Swap every two adjacent nodes (1→2→3→4 becomes 2→1→4→3) without changing values.

Spot it: it's k-group reversal with k = 2, small enough to write the three re-links by hand.

Key insight: with prev_node → first → second → rest, set first.next = rest, second.next = first, prev_node.next = second. Then first is the new prev_node.

Approach:

  1. dummy → head; prev_node = dummy.
  2. While two nodes first, second follow prev_node: first.next = second.next, second.next = first, prev_node.next = second.
  3. Move prev_node to first (now the second node of the pair).
  4. Return dummy.next.
class Solution:
    def swapPairs(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # The head changes (the 2nd node becomes the 1st), so use a dummy.
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        # prev_node = the node just BEFORE the pair we are about to swap.
        prev_node = dummy
        # A pair needs two nodes after prev_node.
        while prev_node.next is not None and prev_node.next.next is not None:
            # Name the two nodes of the pair.
            first = prev_node.next
            second = prev_node.next.next
            # first skips ahead to whatever comes after the pair.
            first.next = second.next
            # second points back to first.
            second.next = first
            # The node before the pair now points to second (the new front).
            prev_node.next = second
            # first is now the back of the pair, so it is the node
            # before the next pair.
            prev_node = first
        return dummy.next

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. dummy = ListNode(0, head): the second node will become the head, so we use a fake node in front and return dummy.next at the end.
  2. prev_node = dummy: the node just before the pair we are about to swap.
  3. while prev_node.next is not None and prev_node.next.next is not None: only swap if two nodes follow prev_node. A single leftover node stays where it is.
  4. first = prev_node.next and second = prev_node.next.next give the two nodes of the pair names.
  5. first.next = second.next: first skips ahead to whatever comes after the pair.
  6. second.next = first: second now points back at first.
  7. prev_node.next = second: the node before the pair now points at second, the new front of the pair.
  8. prev_node = first: first is now the back of the pair, so it is the node before the next pair.

Dry run on LeetCode example head = [1,2,3,4] (expected [2,1,4,3]):

Pairprev_node (before pair)firstsecondlist after the swap
startdummy——1 → 2 → 3 → 4
1dummy122 → 1 → 3 → 4 (prev_node → 1)
21342 → 1 → 4 → 3 (prev_node → 3)
stop3fewer than 2 nodes after prev_node → return 2 → 1 → 4 → 3

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 2130. Maximum Twin Sum of a Linked List

Problem: In a list of even length n, node i and node n−1−i are twins. Return the largest twin sum.

Spot it: you need to walk the first half forwards and the second half backwards at the same time. Reverse the second half in place.

Key insight: find the start of the second half with fast & slow, reverse from there, then walk both halves together.

Approach:

  1. Fast/slow puts slow on the first node of the second half.
  2. Reverse the second half starting at slow.
  3. Walk one pointer from head and one from the reversed half together, adding twin values.
  4. Return the maximum sum.
class Solution:
    def pairSum(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> int:
        # --- 1) Find the first node of the second half (fast & slow). ---
        slow = head
        fast = head
        while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
            slow = slow.next          # slow moves 1 step
            fast = fast.next.next     # fast moves 2 steps
        # slow is now the first node of the second half.

        # --- 2) Reverse the second half, starting at slow. ---
        prev_node = None
        current = slow
        while current is not None:
            next_node = current.next      # save
            current.next = prev_node      # flip
            prev_node = current           # step
            current = next_node           # step
        # prev_node is the head of the reversed second half (the old last node).

        # --- 3) Walk both halves together and add the twins. ---
        best = 0
        front = head          # walks the first half forwards
        back = prev_node      # walks the second half "backwards"
        while back is not None:
            twin_sum = front.val + back.val
            # Keep the biggest sum seen so far.
            if twin_sum > best:
                best = twin_sum
            front = front.next
            back = back.next
        return best

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Phase 1: slow and fast both start at the head. Each round slow moves 1 node and fast moves 2. When fast can't move two more nodes, slow is on the first node of the second half (the list has even length).
  2. Phase 2: reverse the second half with save / flip / step / step, starting at slow. Afterwards prev_node is the old last node, which is now the head of the reversed second half.
  3. Phase 3: front walks the first half from the head; back walks the reversed second half. Node i meets its twin n − 1 − i at the same time.
  4. twin_sum = front.val + back.val, and the if twin_sum > best block keeps the largest sum seen so far.
  5. Both pointers step forward; the loop ends when back runs out. Return best.

1 find middleslow = 2, fast = Noneslow +1, fast +2

2 reverseflipped 1, next_node = Nonereversed half: 1 → 2

Easy 206. Reverse Linked List (iterative + recursive)

Problem: Reverse the entire list and return the new head.

Spot it: template A word for word. Interviewers often ask for the recursive version too.

Recursive insight: reverse everything after head; now head.next is the tail of that reversed part, so hang head after it: head.next.next = head, and cut head.next = None.

Approach:

  1. Iterative: prev_node = None, current = head; repeat save / flip / step / step until current is None; return prev_node.
  2. Recursive base case: an empty or single-node list is its own reverse.
  3. Reverse the rest; head.next is now the last node of that reversed part.
  4. Call the node after head second; set second.next = head (that is head.next.next = head) and head.next = None, then return the head found by the recursion.
class Solution:
    def reverseList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Iterative version: template A.
        prev_node = None          # nothing reversed yet
        current = head            # start flipping at the head
        while current is not None:
            next_node = current.next      # 1. save the rest of the list
            current.next = prev_node      # 2. flip the arrow backwards
            prev_node = current           # 3. step prev_node forward
            current = next_node           # 4. step current forward
        # The old tail is the new head.
        return prev_node

    def reverseListRecursive(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Base case: an empty list or a single node is already reversed.
        if head is None or head.next is None:
            return head
        # Reverse everything AFTER head. new_head is the old last node.
        new_head = self.reverseListRecursive(head.next)
        # head.next still points to the node that came right after head.
        # That node is now the TAIL of the reversed rest.
        second = head.next
        # Hang head after it: the node after me now points back to me.
        second.next = head
        # head is the new tail (for now), so it must point at nothing.
        head.next = None
        return new_head

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. reverseList (iterative): prev_node = None (nothing reversed yet) and current = head.
  2. Inside while current is not None: do the four lines in order: save next_node = current.next, flip current.next = prev_node, step prev_node = current, step current = next_node.
  3. When current becomes None, prev_node is the old tail = new head, so return it.
  4. reverseListRecursive: base case: if the list is empty or has one node, it is already reversed, so return head.
  5. new_head = self.reverseListRecursive(head.next) trusts the recursion to reverse everything after head. new_head is the old last node and never changes on the way back up.
  6. second = head.next: this node was right after head, and after the recursive call it is the tail of the reversed rest.
  7. second.next = head hangs head after it; head.next = None makes head the new tail (otherwise we would get a 2-node cycle).
  8. Return new_head so every level passes the same new head upwards.

8. Common mistakes

Flipping before savingWriting current.next = prev_node before next_node = current.next loses the rest of the list forever.
Returning head or currentAfter the loop, current is None and head is the new tail. Return prev_node.
No dummy node for partial reversalIf left = 1, there's no "node before". A dummy removes that special case, so return dummy.next.
Forgetting to stitch the endsAfter reversing a part, connect the node before it to the new front and the new tail to the node after it. Otherwise you get a cut-off list or a cycle.
Reversing an incomplete last group (k-group)Check that k nodes exist before reversing.

9. Self-check quiz

Inside the reversal loop, which line must come first?

Save before you flip; otherwise the reference to the rest of the list is overwritten.

After while current is not None: finishes, which variable holds the new head?

current is None; prev_node is the last node processed, the old tail.

You're reversing positions 1..3. What makes the code free of special cases?

The dummy guarantees a "node before the part" even when the part starts at the head. Return dummy.next.

Check whether a linked list is a palindrome using O(1) extra space.

Find the middle with fast/slow, reverse the second half in place, then compare the two halves node by node.

Medium 234. Palindrome Linked List (O(1) space)

Problem: Do the list's values read the same forwards and backwards, using only O(1) extra space?

Spot it: Comparing the front with the back means reading the second half backwards. Reverse it in place instead of copying into an array.

Approach:

  1. Find the start of the second half with fast & slow.
  2. Reverse the second half with save / flip / step / step.
  3. Walk from head and from the reversed half together, comparing values.
  4. Any mismatch → False; otherwise True.
class Solution:
    def isPalindrome(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> bool:
        # --- 1) Move slow to the start of the second half (fast & slow). ---
        slow = head
        fast = head
        while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
            slow = slow.next          # 1 step
            fast = fast.next.next     # 2 steps

        # --- 2) Reverse the second half in place. ---
        prev_node = None
        current = slow
        while current is not None:
            next_node = current.next      # save
            current.next = prev_node      # flip
            prev_node = current           # step
            current = next_node           # step

        # --- 3) Walk both halves together and compare values. ---
        front = head          # start of the first half
        back = prev_node      # start of the reversed second half
        while back is not None:
            if front.val != back.val:
                # One mismatch is enough: not a palindrome.
                return False
            front = front.next
            back = back.next
        # Every pair matched.
        return True

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Phase 1: slow moves 1 node per round and fast moves 2. When fast can't continue, slow is at the start of the second half (for odd length it is the middle node, which is fine: it compares with itself).
  2. Phase 2: reverse the second half in place with save / flip / step / step, starting at slow. Afterwards prev_node is the head of the reversed second half.
  3. Phase 3: front starts at the head and back at prev_node. While back still has nodes, compare the values.
  4. if front.val != back.val: return False: one mismatch is enough to prove it is not a palindrome.
  5. Otherwise step both pointers. If the loop ends without a mismatch, every pair matched, so return True.

Medium 143. Reorder List

Problem: Rearrange L0 → L1 → … → Ln into L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln−1 → … by changing links only.

Spot it: You need the back half in reverse order → split at the middle, reverse the second half, then weave.

Approach:

  1. Fast/slow with while fast.next and fast.next.next puts slow at the end of the first half.
  2. Cut after slow and reverse the second half.
  3. Weave: front.next = back, back.next = front_next, then advance both.
  4. Stop when the (shorter or equal) second half runs out.
class Solution:
    def reorderList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> None:
        # 0 or 1 node: nothing to reorder.
        if head is None or head.next is None:
            return

        # --- 1) Move slow to the END of the first half. ---
        slow = head
        fast = head
        while fast.next is not None and fast.next.next is not None:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next

        # --- 2) Cut the list in two and reverse the second half. ---
        prev_node = None
        current = slow.next       # the second half starts after slow
        slow.next = None          # cut: the first half now ends at slow
        while current is not None:
            next_node = current.next      # save
            current.next = prev_node      # flip
            prev_node = current           # step
            current = next_node           # step

        # --- 3) Weave the halves: front1, back1, front2, back2, ... ---
        front = head
        back = prev_node
        while back is not None:
            # Remember where each half continues before we change links.
            front_next = front.next
            back_next = back.next
            # front -> back -> (old front.next)
            front.next = back
            back.next = front_next
            # Move both pointers to their saved next nodes.
            front = front_next
            back = back_next

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. if head is None or head.next is None: return: 0 or 1 nodes, nothing to reorder.
  2. Phase 1: with the condition fast.next is not None and fast.next.next is not None, slow stops at the end of the first half (the first half gets the extra node when the length is odd).
  3. Phase 2: current = slow.next is the start of the second half; slow.next = None cuts the list into two separate lists. Then save / flip / step / step reverses the second half, and prev_node is its new head.
  4. Phase 3 (weave): front walks the first half and back the reversed second half. Before changing links, save front_next and back_next.
  5. front.next = back and back.next = front_next put one back-node between two front-nodes.
  6. Move front and back to their saved next nodes. The loop ends when the second half (never longer than the first) runs out.

Dry run on LeetCode example head = [1,2,3,4,5] (expected [1,5,2,4,3]):

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 61. Rotate List

Problem: Rotate the list to the right by k places: the last k nodes move to the front.

Spot it: Re-linking pointers in place, like reversal. The trick is to close the list into a ring and cut it at the right spot.

Approach:

  1. Measure the length and find the tail.
  2. shift = k % length; if it's 0, return head unchanged.
  3. Link tail.next = head to make a ring.
  4. Walk length − shift − 1 steps from head to the new tail; the new head is new_tail.next; then cut the ring.
class Solution:
    def rotateRight(self, head: Optional[ListNode], k: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # 0 or 1 node: rotating changes nothing.
        if head is None or head.next is None:
            return head

        # --- 1) Measure the length and find the tail. ---
        length = 1
        tail = head
        while tail.next is not None:
            tail = tail.next
            length = length + 1

        # --- 2) Rotating by 'length' places changes nothing, so drop full turns. ---
        # shift = how many places we really need to rotate.
        shift = k % length
        if shift == 0:
            return head

        # --- 3) Close the list into a ring. ---
        tail.next = head

        # --- 4) The new tail is length - shift - 1 steps from the head. ---
        new_tail = head
        for step in range(length - shift - 1):
            new_tail = new_tail.next
        # The node after the new tail is the new head.
        new_head = new_tail.next
        # Cut the ring open.
        new_tail.next = None
        return new_head

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. if head is None or head.next is None: return head: 0 or 1 nodes can't change by rotating.
  2. length = 1, tail = head, then walk tail to the last node, adding 1 to length per step.
  3. shift = k % length: rotating by length places gives the same list back, so only the remainder matters. If shift is 0, return head unchanged.
  4. tail.next = head closes the list into a ring.
  5. The last shift nodes must move to the front, so the new tail is the node at position length − shift, which is length − shift − 1 steps from the head. The for step in range(length - shift - 1) loop walks there.
  6. new_head = new_tail.next, then new_tail.next = None cuts the ring open. Return new_head.

Dry run on LeetCode example head = [1,2,3,4,5], k = 2 (expected [4,5,1,2,3]):

Medium 445. Add Two Numbers II

Problem: Two non-negative numbers are stored as lists with the most-significant digit first. Return their sum as a list in the same order.

Spot it: Addition starts from the least-significant digit, which is at the end. Reverse both lists in place first.

Key insight: Build the answer by prepending each new digit node. It comes out most-significant first, so no final reversal is needed.

Approach:

  1. Reverse both input lists (template A).
  2. Add digit by digit with a carry: digit = total % 10 and carry = total // 10.
  3. Prepend a node for digit to the result.
  4. Continue while either list or the carry remains.
class Solution:
    def addTwoNumbers(self, l1: Optional[ListNode], l2: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # --- 1) Reverse both lists so the ones digit comes first. ---
        first = self.reverse_list(l1)
        second = self.reverse_list(l2)

        # --- 2) Add digit by digit, like on paper, keeping a carry. ---
        carry = 0
        result = None             # the answer list, built from the back
        while first is not None or second is not None or carry != 0:
            total = carry
            # Add the digit from the first number, if it still has digits.
            if first is not None:
                total = total + first.val
                first = first.next
            # Add the digit from the second number, if it still has digits.
            if second is not None:
                total = total + second.val
                second = second.next
            digit = total % 10        # the digit we write down
            carry = total // 10       # the 1 we carry to the next column
            # PREPEND the new digit: put it in front of the answer so far.
            # The answer then comes out most-significant digit first.
            new_node = ListNode(digit)
            new_node.next = result
            result = new_node
        return result

    def reverse_list(self, head):
        # Template A: save, flip, step, step.
        prev_node = None
        current = head
        while current is not None:
            next_node = current.next
            current.next = prev_node
            prev_node = current
            current = next_node
        return prev_node

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. first = self.reverse_list(l1) and second = self.reverse_list(l2): the helper method at the bottom is template A. After reversing, each list starts with its ones digit, which is where adding starts.
  2. carry = 0 and result = None: no carry yet and an empty answer list.
  3. while first is not None or second is not None or carry != 0: keep going while either number still has digits or a carry is left over (e.g. 99 + 1 needs an extra digit).
  4. total = carry, then each if block adds that number's digit (only if it still has one) and moves its pointer forward. This replaces the compact a.val if a else 0 trick.
  5. digit = total % 10 is the digit we write down; carry = total // 10 is the 1 (or 0) carried to the next column.
  6. new_node.next = result then result = new_node prepends the digit. We produce digits ones-first, and prepending each one puts the answer most-significant-first, as required.
  7. Return result.

Dry run on LeetCode example l1 = [7,2,4,3], l2 = [5,6,4] (7243 + 564 = 7807, expected [7,8,0,7]):

Medium 2074. Reverse Nodes in Even Length Groups

Problem: Split the list into consecutive groups of sizes 1, 2, 3, … (the last group may be shorter). Reverse every group whose actual length is even.

Spot it: Reversing chunks in place → k-group reversal where k grows each time and a parity check decides whether to reverse.

Approach:

  1. group_prev = head (group 1 has size 1 and is never reversed); group_size = 2.
  2. Count up to group_size nodes after group_prev to get the group's real length.
  3. If it's even, reverse those nodes with prev_node starting at group_next (the node after the group), set group_prev.next = prev_node, and move group_prev to group_first (the old first node).
  4. If it's odd, move group_prev to group_last (the group's last node).
  5. group_size = group_size + 1; repeat until no nodes remain.
class Solution:
    def reverseEvenLengthGroups(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Group 1 is just the head (size 1, odd), so it is never reversed.
        # group_prev = the node just BEFORE the current group.
        group_prev = head
        group_size = 2            # the size the next group SHOULD have
        while group_prev.next is not None:
            # --- 1) Count the real length of this group (the last may be shorter). ---
            group_last = group_prev
            count = 0
            while count < group_size and group_last.next is not None:
                group_last = group_last.next
                count = count + 1

            if count % 2 == 0:
                # --- 2a) Even length: reverse the group (like k-group). ---
                group_first = group_prev.next
                group_next = group_last.next
                # Start prev_node at group_next so the old first node
                # ends up pointing at the rest of the list.
                prev_node = group_next
                current = group_first
                while current is not group_next:
                    next_node = current.next      # save
                    current.next = prev_node      # flip
                    prev_node = current           # step
                    current = next_node           # step
                # Stitch the front: prev_node is the old last node = new first node.
                group_prev.next = prev_node
                # The old first node is now the group's tail.
                group_prev = group_first
            else:
                # --- 2b) Odd length: leave it alone, just jump over it. ---
                group_prev = group_last

            # The next group should be one node longer.
            group_size = group_size + 1
        return head

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. group_prev = head: group 1 is just the head. Its size is 1 (odd), so it is never reversed, and the head never changes. That's why no dummy is needed.
  2. group_size = 2: the size the next group should have. It grows by 1 after every group.
  3. while group_prev.next is not None: continue while there are nodes after the last finished group.
  4. Count the real length: walk group_last forward up to group_size nodes, counting them in count. The last group may be shorter, which is why we use count (not group_size) to decide.
  5. Even count: name group_first and group_next, then reverse with save / flip / step / step, starting prev_node at group_next (same trick as problem 25) so the old first node points at the rest of the list.
  6. group_prev.next = prev_node stitches the front (prev_node is the old last node = new first). group_prev = group_first, because the old first node is now the group's tail.
  7. Odd count: leave the group alone and jump over it: group_prev = group_last.
  8. group_size = group_size + 1, then do the next group. Return head at the end.
